title: Nicole Burroughs
text: Welcome All! I’m a PhD candidate in the Microbiology program at North Carolina State University. During my time in the Diversity in Changing Environments (DICE) Lab, I’ve developed my interests in coexistence theory and community assembly within microbial systems. I earned a bachelor’s degree in biology and photo & video journalism from the University of North Carolina in 2019 and a Master’s in the Climate Change and Society program at NCSU in 2021. My work in between degrees has allowed me to use this interdisciplinary framework to communicate science to diverse, public audiences. As for my PhD, what better way to get people excited about microbes than studying the ones that function as the gut of a carnivorous plant? My current research asks questions about the maintenance of protozoan diversity in the discrete, multi-trophic communities that assemble within the cup-shaped leaves of Sarracenia purpurea (purple pitcher plant). When I’m not in the lab, or knee-deep in a bog, you can find me sweating it out at the gym, puttering about the garden, or absolutely covered in dog fur.

title: Research
text:
How do species coexist?




Across Earth’s ecosystems, we find an extraordinary diversity of life. Some species sharing a habitat are strikingly different from one another, like a deer and an oak tree. Others are remarkably similar, like Monarch and Viceroy butterflies. Yet whether they are very different or nearly indistinguishable, neighboring species must find ways to coexist in environments where space, food, and other resources are limited.
So why do some species persist alongside one another, while others are outcompeted and disappear?
My research explores these questions using the tiny aquatic ecosystems that form inside the leaves of purple pitcher plants. These carnivorous plants collect rainwater in their cup-shaped leaves, creating miniature habitats inhabited by a diverse community of microorganisms. Among these are approximately 45 species of protists (single-celled organisms with complex cell structures) that interact, compete, and coexist within the pitcher plant food web.
By studying this relatively simple community of closely interacting species, I can experimentally test ecological theories about competition, coexistence, and community assembly. We’ve got about a century of theoretical development research from which to draw mathematical tools for predicting how species interact and whether they can persist together. My goal is to understand how well these predictions hold up against the complexity of real biological communities, and ultimately what these small microbial ecosystems can teach us about the processes that maintain biodiversity in nature.









How well can we predict species interaction outcomes?



When two species rely on similar resources and compete for space, food, or other necessities, sometimes they find a way to persist alongside one another. Other times, one species eventually out-competes the other, and in still others, it depends on the inital conditions in which species are introduced to one another (priority effects).
My research explores this question using five protist species that naturally inhabit pitcher plant leaves. In a laboratory setting, I measured how each species grows on its own and how its growth changed when competing with another species. I used these measurements to build mathematical models that predict what will happen when different pairs of species compete.
Importantly, I did’t stop at making predictions. I conducted separate experiments to see whether the outcomes predicted by my models actually matched what happened when these organisms compete. Our results suggest that ecological theory can often predict whether competing species will coexist, but predicting how much of each species will remain is considerably more challenging.








How do changing temperatures alter coexistence potential and our ability to predict it?



Species interactions don’t happen in isolation from the environment. Temperature, for example, influences how quickly organisms grow, how efficiently they use resources, and how well they tolerate competition. As the world warms and environmental conditions change, the balance of competition between species can shift, potentially changing which species are able to coexist.
Building on my work predicting the outcomes of pairwise competition, I am investigating how temperature influences both species interactions and our ability to predict them. Using the same five species of pitcher plant protists, I plan to repeat my pairwise competition experiments across a range of temperatures, from the lower to upper limits of temperatures the protists experience in their native habitat. I will use these experiments to measure how competition changes across temperatures and evaluate whether mathematical models parameterized under different environmental conditions can accurately predict the resulting community dynamics.
Ultimately, this research asks whether the rules governing species coexistence remain consistent as environmental conditions change, or whether shifts in temperature fundamentally alter the outcome of competition.








How predictable is community assembly?



Biodiversity isn’t distributed evenly across a landscape. Even when neighboring habitats are physically similar, they can develop surprisingly different communities of organisms. Predicting community assembly requires understanding how dispersal, spatial structure, and historical contingency interact in natural systems.
Because individual pitcher leaves offer relatively similar environments but can develop different microbial communities, they provide a natural system for investigating community assembly. To understand how these differences arise, I pair sterilized “recipient” pitchers with neighboring, undisturbed “donor” pitchers in a native bog and track community development over time. By characterizing variation in established donor communities and comparing it with the communities that develop in recipient pitchers, I can investigate how the diversity of existing communities influences the range of assembly outcomes in newly available habitats.
Ultimately, this research asks whether ecological communities assemble according to predictable rules or whether their trajectories are fundamentally contingent on the circumstances of their formation. Understanding the balance between these processes is essential for predicting how biodiversity is distributed across landscapes and how ecological communities might respond to environmental change.
